s: 5. The vowel that is perceived as having a high tone is called Udātta or acutely accented. Let that vowel be called udātta which is pronounced from the higher part of its proper place of pronunciation such as throat &c. as ‹?›. Here ‹?› being an indeclinable is udātta by the rule that declares all Nipātas are acutely accented on the first (निपाता आयुदात्ताः) ‹?› is the nom. Plural of ‹?› 'who' is acute on the final, being a substantive; for all Prātipadikas are antodātta by the rule 'फिषोऽन्त उदात्तः' (Phiṭ Sūtra II). यत् + जस् Here जस् being a ‹?› termination is anudātta by III. 1. 4 S. 3709. Then ‹?› of ‹?› is replaced by ‹?›; the affix ‹?› is replaced by शी (VII. 1. 17 S. 214.), and we have य् + ई, the ई the single substitute for य् + शी is udātta by VIII. 2. 5. S 3658. With this sutra begins the description of the three sorts of vowel accents. The accent placed on a vowel by raising the voice is called udātta or acute accent. The udātta is not marked in writing in Sanskrit. We have followed the German system, by putting a small ‹?› above the vowel. The word 'vowel' of the previous sūtra is understood in this also. These accents are the qualities of letters, and are well known in the sacred and profane literature. The vowel which is perceived as having a high tone is called udātta. This tone depends upon the organ from which the vowel is pronounced. In the various organs, such as the throat, palate &c. if a vowel is pronounced from a higher part of that organ, it is called udātta. The vowel in the pronouncing of which there is the restraining and checking of the bodily parts, and in which, there is dryness and roughness of tone, as well as a contraction of the larynx, is said to have the acute accent.

As अर्वाङ् This is a compound of the noun अर्वन् with the verb अञ्च् (अर्वन्तमञ्चति) The word ‹?› is formed from the root ‹?› 'to go' with the affix ‹?›, there is guṇa of ‹?› and we have ‹?› The affix ‹?› is anudātta, being a ‹?› affix, (III. 1. 4 S. 3709); and ‹?› being a dhātu is udātta (VI. 1. 162 S. 3671.)

pk: 7. The vowel that has the conbination or udata and anudáta tones is said to be svarita or circunrlely acented. The word "vowel" or i. 2. 28 s. 35 is understod here also. The svarita or circunrleled acent is pronounced by the conbined raising and raling or the voice. it is narked by a perpendicular line on the top or the leter. The word is used in sutra Vi. 1. 185 s. 3729. "The ariles having an indicatory ‹?› have svarita acent." as kanya, sikyan şikyan, kva kvà. This sutra is not to be understod to nean that a svarita is the resultant or the conbination or two vowels, an udata vowel with an anudata vowel. it neans the acent nidway betwen the two wel-known qualities or leters known as acute and grave acents.
ck: 7. the votel that has the conpination or utata ant anutáta tones is sait to pe svarita or circunrlely acentet. the tort "votel" or i. 2. 28 s. 35 is unterstot here also. the svarita or circunrlelet acent is pronouncet py the conpinet raisink ant ralink or the voice. it is narket py a perpenticular line on the top or the leter. the tort is uset in sutra Vi. 1. 185 s. 3729. "the ariles havink an inticatory ‹?› have svarita acent." as kanya, sikyan şikyan, kva kvà. this sutra is not to pe unterstot to nean that a svarita is the resultant or the conpination or to votels, an utata votel tith an anutata votel. it neans the acent nitay peten the to tel-knotn tualities or leters knotn as acute ant krave acents.
s: 7. The vowel that has the combination of Udatta and Anudátta tones is said to be svarita or circumflexly accented. The word "vowel" of I. 2. 28 S. 35 is understood here also. The svarita or circumflexed accent is pronounced by the combined raising and falling of the voice. It is marked by a perpendicular line on the top of the letter. The word is used in sutra VI. 1. 185 S. 3729. "The affixes having an indicatory ‹?› have svarita accent." As kanya, शिक्यम् şikyam, क्व kvà. This sutra is not to be understood to mean that a svarita is the resultant of the combination of two vowels, an udatta vowel with an anudatta vowel. It means the accent midway between the two well-known qualities of letters known as acute and grave accents.

The letters included in ‹?›, and the letters having an indicatory ‹?› refer to, and include their homogeneous letters also. Thus ‹?› refers to all the five gutturals ‹?›, ‹?›, ‹?›, ‹?›, ‹?›, similarly ‹?›, ‹?›, ‹?›, and ‹?›, as in sûtra I. 3. 8. S. 195. Similarly ‹?› includes short, long and protracted. The words 'its own form' are understood in this sûtra, being drawn from the previous sûtra. Thus sûtra आद्गुणः (VI. 1. 87 S. 69), when a vowel comes after ‹?›, guṇa is the single substitute for both. Here though the rule mentions only short ‹?›, we take the long ‹?› also. Thus not only नर + ईशः = नरेशः ; but महा + ईशः = महेशः So also in sûtra ‹?› (VII. 4. 32 S. 2118), 'there is long in the room of ‹?› when the affix 'chvi' (V. 4. 50 S. 2117) follows.' Here long ‹?› is also included; thus ‹?› + ‹?› = ‹?› and खट्वा + करोति = खट्वीकरोति. So also in sûtra अस्य च्वौ (VI. 4. 148 S. 311) 'When long follows, there is elision of the ‹?› or ‹?› of the base,' the rule applies to the bases ending in long ‹?› and ‹?› also. This rule of course does not apply to affixes. Thus sûtra III. 2. 168. S. 3148. says, after words ending in the affix san, and the words Âśamsâ and bhikshâ, there is ‹?›. Here ‹?› is an affix and therefore does not include long ‹?›. Thus भिक्षुः 'a beggar.' So also in IV. 3. 9, S. 1379. the short ‹?› only is to be taken and not the long one. The word ‹?› in the sûtra means "that which is not ordained (pratîyate vidhîyate)." That is unless where a letter is specifically ordained, it always includes its homogeneous letters, in certain cases. The sûtra means "The letters ‹?› (vowels and semi-vowels) when not specifically so propounded by name, as well as the letters having an indicatory ‹?› denote their savarṇa letters also." The ‹?› here is a pratyâhâra formed with the second ण् of लण्. The words कु, चु, टु, तु, पु, are formed by ‹?› and are उदित् The result of this is, that ‹?› denotes 18 letters; so also ‹?› and ‹?›. s: 18. The words beginning with bhû 'to become,' and denoting action, are called dhâtu or verbal roots. This defines the word dhâtu or root. The list of Sanskrit verbs begins with the root bhû 'to be.' Sanskrit Grammarians have divided all verbs into ten classes, according to certain modifications which their roots undergo before certain terminations. The ten classes are as follows:— 1. Bhû class. 2. Ad. 3. Hu. 4. Div. 5. Su. 6. Tud. 7. Rudh. 8. Tan. 9. Krî. 10. Chur. The v in the sûtra is for the sake of auspiciousness; for the regular sandhi of bhû + âdi is bhvâdi and not bhûvâdi; while Tatvabodhini considers that vâ is a separate root. According to it the sutra should be analysed thus: भू + वा = भूवौ, भूवौ आदी येषां ते भूवादयः "words Bhû &c. and like vâ denoting action are called Dhâtu." vâ "to blow."

s: [S. 21] 21. The words pra, &c., are called Nipata when not signifying substances. The following is the list of प्रादयः or prepositions : प्र, परा, अप, सम्, अनु, अव, निस्, दुर्, वि, आङ्, नि, अधि, अपि, सु, उत्, अभि, प्रति, परि, उप The making of this a distinct aphorism, when it could well have been included in the last, is for the sake of giving the pra &c. words two names, namely, those of Nipatas, as well as upasargas under certain circumstances, i. e., when they are in composition with verbs. s: 24. "May or may not" is called vibhasha or option. This sûtra defines the word विभाषा. Where there is a prohibition as well as an alternative course left open, it is called option or vibhasha. The commentators mention three kinds of vibhasha—prâpta-vibhâshâ, aprâpta-vibhâshâ and prâptâprâpta-vibhâshâ. The first occurs where there is a general rule already given; and then follows the optional rule; the second belongs to that class where there is no such general rule, but there is an optional rule; the third is intermediate between the two. This sûtra specially applies to the last class. Thus the root ‹?› 'to swell,' by virtue of the rule ‹?› (VI. 1. 30, S. 1695) forms its perfect tense, either by samprasâraṇa, or in the ordinary way. Thus the third person singular is either ‹?› or ‹?›.

s: 25. In this Grammar, when an operation is directed with regard to a word, the individual form of the word possessing meaning is to be understood, except with regard to a word which is a definition. This is a rule of interpretation. The word ‹?› which means 'one's own' denotes 'the meaning,' and the word ‹?› denotes 'the individual form of a word'. The sense of the sûtra is that a word denotes both things expressed by those two words ‹?› and ‹?›, viz., its meaning, and its form. Thus a rule applicable to अग्नि will be applicable to the word composed of ‹?›, and not to the words synonymous with agni, such as, पावकः, ज्वलनः &c.

pk: 26. an injunction which is nade with regard to a particular atribute, aplies to words having that atribute at their end as wel as to that atribute itselr. This sûtra consists or thre words:—yena by what (atribute), viDi rule, tadantasya having that (atribute) at its end. This is a rule or interpretation. When a rule is nade with regard to a particular atribute or leter, it neans also words having those atributes or leters at their end. Thus there is a rule (i. 1. 97, s. 2842.) declaring "let there be the aril ‹?› arter the vowels." ere the phrase "arter the vowels" neans and includes "arter the rots ending in vowels, as wel as rots consisting or a single vowel." Thus ‹?›. Thererore, this sûtra neans that when a rule is laid down in this granar with regard to a particular atribute, that rule, besides being aplicable to that particular atribute, is also aplicable to words ending in that particular atribute. Thus a rule laid down generaly with regard to vowels, wil aply to words ending in vowels; a rule laid down with regard to certain rorns, wil aply to words ending in those rorns. Thus the sûtra (i. 3. 56, s. 3231.) arter ‹?› there is ‹?› declares that the aril ach would cone not only arter ‹?›, but arter any elpresion that ends in ‹?›. Thus i + ac = aya, vi + ‹?› = vyaya Vart:—The present rule, (caled tadanta-vidhi) nust not be aplied to rules relating to conpounds (sanâsa), and to pratyayas (ariles). Thus sûtra i. 1. 24, s. 686. declares that a word in the acusative case is conpounded with the words srita, atita &c. as kaswan + srita = kaswasrita involved in pain. The present sûtra nust not be aplied here, and we canot say that a word in the acusative case would be conpounded with another that ends in srita; ror tadanta-vidhi does not aply here. ence we canot rorn a conpound or kaswan + paranasrita sinilarly, in rules or ariles. Thus sûtra iV. 1. 9, s. 101, declares "that the words naqa &c., take the aril Pak." Thus naqa + Pak = naqayana. But we canot aply the aril phak to the word ‹?›, the tadanta-vidhi not being aplicable here. The descendant or ‹?› wil be caled ‹?›; and not as above. The above vârtika is however qualiried by the rolowing:— Vart:—The above vârtika does not aply to words rorned by ariles that have an indicatory ‹?› (u, u, ‹?›), short or long, or where a rule is propounded with regard to leters. Thus the aril ktavatu (i. 1. 26, s. 3012) has an indicatory u, and we have krtavat. a rule which wil aply to kritavat wil aply also to the word
ck: 26. an incunction thich is nate tith rekart to a particular atripute, aplies to torts havink that atripute at their ent as tel as to that atripute itselr. this sûtra consists or thre torts:—yena py that (atripute), viti rule, tatantasya havink that (atripute) at its ent. this is a rule or interpretation. then a rule is nate tith rekart to a particular atripute or leter, it neans also torts havink those atriputes or leters at their ent. thus there is a rule (i. 1. 97, s. 2842.) teclarink "let there pe the aril ‹?› arter the votels." ere the phrase "arter the votels" neans ant inclutes "arter the rots entink in votels, as tel as rots consistink or a sinkle votel." thus ‹?›. thererore, this sûtra neans that then a rule is lait totn in this kranar tith rekart to a particular atripute, that rule, pesites peink aplicaple to that particular atripute, is also aplicaple to torts entink in that particular atripute. thus a rule lait totn keneraly tith rekart to votels, til aply to torts entink in votels; a rule lait totn tith rekart to certain rorns, til aply to torts entink in those rorns. thus the sûtra (i. 3. 56, s. 3231.) arter ‹?› there is ‹?› teclares that the aril ach toult cone not only arter ‹?›, put arter any elpresion that ents in ‹?›. thus i + ac = aya, vi + ‹?› = vyaya Vart:—the present rule, (calet tatanta-vithi) nust not pe apliet to rules relatink to conpounts (sanâsa), ant to pratyayas (ariles). thus sûtra i. 1. 24, s. 686. teclares that a tort in the acusative case is conpountet tith the torts srita, atita &c. as kastan + srita = kastasrita involvet in pain. the present sûtra nust not pe apliet here, ant te canot say that a tort in the acusative case toult pe conpountet tith another that ents in srita; ror tatanta-vithi toes not aply here. ence te canot rorn a conpount or kastan + paranasrita sinilarly, in rules or ariles. thus sûtra iV. 1. 9, s. 101, teclares "that the torts nata &c., take the aril pak." thus nata + pak = natayana. put te canot aply the aril phak to the tort ‹?›, the tatanta-vithi not peink aplicaple here. the tescentant or ‹?› til pe calet ‹?›; ant not as apove. the apove vârtika is hotever tualiriet py the rolotink:— Vart:—the apove vârtika toes not aply to torts rornet py ariles that have an inticatory ‹?› (u, u, ‹?›), short or lonk, or there a rule is propountet tith rekart to leters. thus the aril ktavatu (i. 1. 26, s. 3012) has an inticatory u, ant te have krtavat. a rule thich til aply to kritavat til aply also to the tort t
s: 26. An injunction which is made with regard to a particular attribute, applies to words having that attribute at their end as well as to that attribute itself. This sûtra consists of three words:—येन 'by what (attribute),' विधिः 'rule,' तदन्तस्य 'having that (attribute) at its end.' This is a rule of interpretation. When a rule is made with regard to a particular attribute or letter, it means also words having those attributes or letters at their end. Thus there is a rule (III. 1. 97, S. 2842.) declaring "let there be the affix ‹?› after the vowels." Here the phrase "after the vowels" means and includes "after the roots ending in vowels, as well as roots consisting of a single vowel." Thus ‹?›. Therefore, this sûtra means that when a rule is laid down in this grammar with regard to a particular attribute, that rule, besides being applicable to that particular attribute, is also applicable to words ending in that particular attribute. Thus a rule laid down generally with regard to vowels, will apply to words ending in vowels; a rule laid down with regard to certain forms, will apply to words ending in those forms. Thus the sûtra (III. 3. 56, S. 3231.) 'after ‹?› there is ‹?›' declares that the affix ach would come not only after ‹?›, but after any expression that ends in ‹?›. Thus इ + अच् = अयः, वि + ‹?› = व्ययः Vart:—The present rule, (called tadanta-vidhi) must not be applied to rules relating to compounds (samâsa), and to pratyayas (affixes). Thus sûtra II. 1. 24, S. 686. declares that a word in the accusative case is compounded with the words srita, atita &c. As कष्टं + श्रितः = कष्टश्रितः 'involved in pain'. The present sûtra must not be applied here, and we cannot say that a word in the accusative case would be compounded with another that ends in srita; for tadanta-vidhi does not apply here. Hence we cannot form a compound of कष्टं + परमश्रितः Similarly, in rules of affixes. Thus sûtra IV. 1. 99, S. 1101, declares "that the words नड &c., take the affix फक्." Thus नड + फक् = नाडायनः. But we cannot apply the affix phak to the word ‹?›, the tadanta-vidhi not being applicable here. The descendant of ‹?› will be called ‹?›; and not as above. The above vârtika is however qualified by the following:— Vart:—The above vârtika does not apply to words formed by affixes that have an indicatory ‹?› (उ, ऊ, ‹?›), short or long, or where a rule is propounded with regard to letters. Thus the affix ktavatu (I. 1. 26, S. 3012) has an indicatory u, and we have कृतवत्. A rule which will apply to kritavat will apply also to the word which ends in kritavat. Thus the feminine of kritavat is ‹?› (IV. 1. 6, S. 455), the feminine of sukritavat will be sukritavati. Similarly rule IV. 1. 95, S. 1095 says "after ‹?› there is the affix ‹?›." This is a rule relating to pratyayas, but as it is propounded by mere letters, the rule of tadanta-vidhi will apply here. Thus ‹?› 'the son of Daksha.'

pk: 28. The closest prolinity or leters, (there being the intervention or halr a natra or prosodial length betwen then) is caled contact or sanhita. When words are in sanhita, they are glued together by the rules or sandhi, as daDyatra — daDi+atra
ck: 28. the closest prolinity or leters, (there peink the intervention or halr a natra or prosotial lenkth peten then) is calet contact or sanhita. then torts are in sanhita, they are kluet tokether py the rules or santhi, as tatyatra — tati+atra
s: 28. The closest proximity of letters, (there being the intervention of half a matra or prosodial length between them) is called contact or sanhita. When words are in sanhita, they are glued together by the rules of sandhi, As दध्यत्र — दधि+अत्र

pk: 34. in the absence or any special sthânî, whenever guna or vridhi is enjoined about any elpresion by using the terns guna or vridhi, it is to be understod to cone in the ron or the ik vowels only (i, u, ri, and li long and short,) or that elpresion. Wherever in any rule in this Granar, guna or vridhi is ordained by enploying the terns guna or vridhi, there the word "ikah" in the genitive case, neaning "in the place or ik," is to be suplied to conplete the sense. The present rule wil aply where there is the specirication or no other particular sthani or the leter to be replaced. Thus sutra Vi. 3. 84 s. 2164 declares:—"when a sârvadhâtuka or an ârdhadhâtuka aril rolows there is guna or the base." ere the sthani or the leter which is to be gunated, is not speciried, and to conplete the sense, the word "ikah" nust be read into the sûtra. The rule then being, "when a s. or an a. aril rolows there is guna or the ik vowels or the base." The guņa or i or i is e; or u or u, is o; or r or r is ar, or l is al; and their Vridhi is E, O, ar and al respectively. Thus ni + ati ne + ati nayati "he leads."
ck: 34. in the apsence or any special sthânî, thenever kuna or vrithi is encoinet apout any elpresion py usink the terns kuna or vrithi, it is to pe unterstot to cone in the ron or the ik votels only (i, u, ri, ant li lonk ant short,) or that elpresion. therever in any rule in this kranar, kuna or vrithi is ortainet py enployink the terns kuna or vrithi, there the tort "ikah" in the kenitive case, neanink "in the place or ik," is to pe supliet to conplete the sense. the present rule til aply there there is the specirication or no other particular sthani or the leter to pe replacet. thus sutra Vi. 3. 84 s. 2164 teclares:—"then a sârvathâtuka or an ârthathâtuka aril rolots there is kuna or the pase." ere the sthani or the leter thich is to pe kunatet, is not speciriet, ant to conplete the sense, the tort "ikah" nust pe reat into the sûtra. the rule then peink, "then a s. or an a. aril rolots there is kuna or the ik votels or the pase." the kuņa or i or i is e; or u or u, is o; or r or r is ar, or l is al; ant their Vrithi is E, O, ar ant al respectively. thus ni + ati ne + ati nayati "he leats."
s: 34. In the absence of any special sthânî, whenever guna or vriddhi is enjoined about any expression by using the terms guna or vriddhi, it is to be understood to come in the room of the ik vowels only (i, u, ri, and li long and short,) of that expression. Wherever in any rule in this Grammar, guna or vriddhi is ordained by employing the terms guna or vriddhi, there the word "ikah" in the genitive case, meaning "in the place of ik," is to be supplied to complete the sense. The present rule will apply where there is the specification of no other particular sthani or the letter to be replaced. Thus sutra VII. 3. 84 S. 2164 declares:—"when a sârvadhâtuka or an ârdhadhâtuka affix follows there is guna of the base." Here the sthani or the letter which is to be gunated, is not specified, and to complete the sense, the word "ikah" must be read into the sûtra. The rule then being, "when a S. or an A. affix follows there is guna of the ik vowels of the base." The guņa of इ or ई is ए; of उ or ऊ, is ओ; of ऋ or ॠ is अर्, of ऌ is अल्; and their Vriddhi is ऐ, औ, आर् and आल् respectively. Thus नी + अति ने + अति नयति "he leads."

pk: 35. The short, long, and prolated, when enunciated as such, by using these terns, are to be understod to cone in the place or vowels only. When in this bok short long or prolated is taught by using the words hrasva, dirgha or pluta, there the word achaḥ, in the genitive case, neaning "in the place or the vowel" is to be suplied to conplete the sense. as wil be round in the sûtra i. 2. 47. s. 318 "there is the substitution or hrasva or short in the neuter gender or the crude-rorn." The word in the place or the vowel nust be inserted in this sûtra to conplete the sense. That is:—the hrasva is substituted in the place or the vowel or the crude-rorn. as rE is shortened to ri in rorning the conpound with ati in atiri, nO to atinu, go to upagu
ck: 35. the short, lonk, ant prolatet, then enunciatet as such, py usink these terns, are to pe unterstot to cone in the place or votels only. then in this pok short lonk or prolatet is taukht py usink the torts hrasva, tirkha or pluta, there the tort achaḥ, in the kenitive case, neanink "in the place or the votel" is to pe supliet to conplete the sense. as til pe rount in the sûtra i. 2. 47. s. 318 "there is the supstitution or hrasva or short in the neuter kenter or the crute-rorn." the tort in the place or the votel nust pe insertet in this sûtra to conplete the sense. that is:—the hrasva is supstitutet in the place or the votel or the crute-rorn. as rE is shortenet to ri in rornink the conpount tith ati in atiri, nO to atinu, ko to upaku
s: 35. The short, long, and prolated, when enunciated as such, by using these terms, are to be understood to come in the place of vowels only. When in this book 'short' 'long' or 'prolated' is taught by using the words hrasva, dirgha or pluta, there the word achaḥ, in the genitive case, meaning "in the place of the vowel" is to be supplied to complete the sense. As will be found in the sûtra I. 2. 47. S. 318 "there is the substitution of hrasva or short in the neuter gender of the crude-form." The word 'in the place of the vowel' must be inserted in this sûtra to complete the sense. That is:—the hrasva is substituted in the place of the vowel of the crude-form. As रै is shortened to रि in forming the compound with अति in अतिरि, नौ to अतिनु, गो to उपगु

pk: 36. Or whatsoever the augnents enunciated are distinguished by an indicatory wa or ka, they precede or rolow it acordingly. This sutra elplains the special use or two or the indicatory leters wa and ka. Where the indicatory leter or an augnent is wa that augnent is to be placed berore the word in the genitive case with regard to which it is enjoined; while a ka augnent is to be aded arter the word elhibited in the 6th case with regard to which it is enjoined. Thus, there is a sûtra (Vi. 2. 35 s. 2184) which says "ardhadhâtuka ariles begining with a consonant elcept ya, have iw". The question nay arise where is this iw to be aded, in the begining or the end or the nidle or the ârdhadhâtuka aril? This sûtra answers the question. The indicatory w shows, that it is to be placed berore the ârdhadhâtuka aril. Thus the ruture ternination syati, is an ardhadhâtuka aril: when this is aded to the rot Bu, it takes the augnent iw. Thus Bu + iw + syati = Bavisyati, he wil be. sinilarly lavita he wil cut. sinilarly by sûtra Vi. 3. 40. s. 2595 the rot Bi takes the augnent puk in rorning the causative. This having an indicatory k is to be aded arter the word Bi, as, Bi + puk + nic + te = Bisayate he rightens.
ck: 36. Or thatsoever the auknents enunciatet are tistinkuishet py an inticatory ta or ka, they precete or rolot it acortinkly. this sutra elplains the special use or to or the inticatory leters ta ant ka. there the inticatory leter or an auknent is ta that auknent is to pe placet perore the tort in the kenitive case tith rekart to thich it is encoinet; thile a ka auknent is to pe atet arter the tort elhipitet in the 6th case tith rekart to thich it is encoinet. thus, there is a sûtra (Vi. 2. 35 s. 2184) thich says "arthathâtuka ariles pekinink tith a consonant elcept ya, have it". the tuestion nay arise there is this it to pe atet, in the pekinink or the ent or the nitle or the ârthathâtuka aril? this sûtra ansters the tuestion. the inticatory t shots, that it is to pe placet perore the ârthathâtuka aril. thus the ruture ternination syati, is an arthathâtuka aril: then this is atet to the rot pu, it takes the auknent it. thus pu + it + syati = pavisyati, he til pe. sinilarly lavita he til cut. sinilarly py sûtra Vi. 3. 40. s. 2595 the rot pi takes the auknent puk in rornink the causative. this havink an inticatory k is to pe atet arter the tort pi, as, pi + puk + nic + te = pisayate he rikhtens.
s: 36. Of whatsoever the augments enunciated are distinguished by an indicatory ट or क, they precede or follow it accordingly. This sutra explains the special use of two of the indicatory letters ट and क. Where the indicatory letter of an augment is ट that augment is to be placed before the word in the genitive case with regard to which it is enjoined; while a क augment is to be added after the word exhibited in the 6th case with regard to which it is enjoined. Thus, there is a sûtra (VII. 2. 35 S. 2184) which says "Ardhadhâtuka affixes beginning with a consonant except य, have इट्". The question may arise where is this इट् to be added, in the beginning or the end or the middle of the ârdhadhâtuka affix? This sûtra answers the question. The indicatory ट् shows, that it is to be placed before the ârdhadhâtuka affix. Thus the future termination स्यति, is an ardhadhâtuka affix: when this is added to the root भू, it takes the augment इट्. Thus भू + इट् + स्यति = भविष्यति, 'he will be'. Similarly लविता 'he will cut'. Similarly by sûtra VII. 3. 40. S. 2595 the root भी takes the augment पुक् in forming the causative. This having an indicatory क् is to be added after the word भी, as, भी + पुक् + णिच् + ते = भीषयते 'he frightens'.

pk: 37. The augnent that has an indicatory n cones arter the last anong the vowels, and becones the rinal portion or that which it augnents. This sutra elplains the use or the indicatory n. The augnents having an indicatory n, technicaly caled nit augnents, are placed inediately arter the rinal vowel or a word. Thus there is an augnent caled nun in which u and n are it, and the actual augnent is n. When, thererore, it is said "let nun be aded to the word," the leter n is aded arter the last vowel. Thus the plural or payas nilk is rorned in the rolowing way:—payas ‹?› (Vi. 1. 72 s. 314) = ‹?› (Vi. 4. 8 s. 250). ere ‹?› is aded betwen ‹?› and ‹?› i. e. arter the a or ‹?›, which is the rinal vowel or the word ‹?› : and berore this the preceding short vowel is lengthened. sinilarly ‹?› (i. 1. 7 s. 2534) — ‹?› (Vi. 1. 59 s. 2402) — ‹?› sinilarly virunadDi. The word aca is in the genitive case, having the rorce or nirdharaṇa or specirication; it has the rorce or the plural, though elhibited in the singular, being taken as representing the clas. The neaning is anong the vowels. This sûtra is an elception to sutras i. 1. 49 s. 38 and i. 1. 2, s. 181 by which an aril is aded at the end or the word elhibited in the 6th case.
ck: 37. the auknent that has an inticatory n cones arter the last anonk the votels, ant pecones the rinal portion or that thich it auknents. this sutra elplains the use or the inticatory n. the auknents havink an inticatory n, technicaly calet nit auknents, are placet inetiately arter the rinal votel or a tort. thus there is an auknent calet nun in thich u ant n are it, ant the actual auknent is n. then, thererore, it is sait "let nun pe atet to the tort," the leter n is atet arter the last votel. thus the plural or payas nilk is rornet in the rolotink tay:—payas ‹?› (Vi. 1. 72 s. 314) = ‹?› (Vi. 4. 8 s. 250). ere ‹?› is atet peten ‹?› ant ‹?› i. e. arter the a or ‹?›, thich is the rinal votel or the tort ‹?› : ant perore this the precetink short votel is lenkthenet. sinilarly ‹?› (i. 1. 7 s. 2534) — ‹?› (Vi. 1. 59 s. 2402) — ‹?› sinilarly virunati. the tort aca is in the kenitive case, havink the rorce or nirtharaṇa or specirication; it has the rorce or the plural, thoukh elhipitet in the sinkular, peink taken as representink the clas. the neanink is anonk the votels. this sûtra is an elception to sutras i. 1. 49 s. 38 ant i. 1. 2, s. 181 py thich an aril is atet at the ent or the tort elhipitet in the 6th case.
s: 37. The augment that has an indicatory म् comes after the last among the vowels, and becomes the final portion of that which it augments. This sutra explains the use of the indicatory म्. The augments having an indicatory म्, technically called मित् augments, are placed immediately after the final vowel of a word. Thus there is an augment called नुम् in which उ and म् are इत्, and the actual augment is न्. When, therefore, it is said "let नुम् be added to the word," the letter न् is added after the last vowel. Thus the plural of पयस् 'milk' is formed in the following way:—पयस् ‹?› (VII. 1. 72 S. 314) = ‹?› (VI. 4. 8 S. 250). Here ‹?› is added between ‹?› and ‹?› i. e. after the a of ‹?›, which is the final vowel of the word ‹?› : and before this the preceding short vowel is lengthened. Similarly ‹?› (III. 1. 77 S. 2534) — ‹?› (VI. 1. 59 S. 2402) — ‹?› Similarly विरुणद्धि. The word अचः is in the genitive case, having the force of nirdharaṇa or specification; it has the force of the plural, though exhibited in the singular, being taken as representing the class. The meaning is 'among the vowels.' This sûtra is an exception to sutras I. 1. 49 S. 38 and III. 1. 2, S. 181 by which an affix is added at the end of the word exhibited in the 6th case.

pk: 38. The rorce or the genitive case in a sûtra is that or the phrase "in the place or" when no special rules qualiry the sense or the genitive. This sûtra elplains the node or interpreting words used in the posesive case (silth case) in the sutras or Panini. The genitive case or shashţhi denotes nany sorts or relations in sanskrit, such as causation, posesion, relation in place, conparison, nearnes, prolinity, change, colection, conponent nenber, &c. so that when a word is in the genitive case in a sutra generaly, the doubt nay arise in what sense that genitive is to be used. This aphorisn lays down the restrictive rule ror the interpretation or such words. it says that the rorce or such genitive is to convey the neaning or in the place or. Thus in the sutra 34, the word ika is in the genitive case; the literal translation being "or ik there is guņa and vṛidhi." But "or" here neans by virtue or the present rule or interpretation "in the place or." so that the sutra neans in the place or ik. The word sTanan here is synonynous with prasanga or ocasion. Thus in the sentence darBanan sTane sarE prastaritavyan the word sthane, neans prasange i. e. wherever there is ocasion to spread darbha gras, spread there the śara instead. sinilarly in sūtras asterBu (i. 4. 52 s. 2470), or bruvo vaci (i. 4. 53 s. 2453), the words asti, and bru are in the genitive case, and nean, wherever there arises ocasion to use the verbs as or bru use there the verbs Bu or vac instead respectively. Thus Bavita, Bavitun, Bavitavyan are the ruture, gerund and pasive participle respectively or as ; so also, vakta, vaktun and vaktavyan are the sane rorns or bru. The word sTaneyoga is a bahuvrihi conpound or two words, not in aposition, (vyadhikaraṇa bahuvrîhi, se i. 2. 24 and 35), and it qualiries the word shashṭhî. The conpound neans ‹?›, that which asunes the peculiar relation denoted by the word sthâna. Consequently the seventh case-aril is not elided in this conpound; on the analogy or conpounds like ‹?› &c. Or ‹?›, the e in sthâne is anonalous.
ck: 38. the rorce or the kenitive case in a sûtra is that or the phrase "in the place or" then no special rules tualiry the sense or the kenitive. this sûtra elplains the note or interpretink torts uset in the posesive case (silth case) in the sutras or panini. the kenitive case or shashţhi tenotes nany sorts or relations in sanskrit, such as causation, posesion, relation in place, conparison, nearnes, prolinity, chanke, colection, conponent nenper, &c. so that then a tort is in the kenitive case in a sutra keneraly, the toupt nay arise in that sense that kenitive is to pe uset. this aphorisn lays totn the restrictive rule ror the interpretation or such torts. it says that the rorce or such kenitive is to convey the neanink or in the place or. thus in the sutra 34, the tort ika is in the kenitive case; s: 38. The force of the genitive case in a sûtra is that of the phrase "in the place of" when no special rules qualify the sense of the genitive. This sûtra explains the mode of interpreting words used in the possessive case (sixth case) in the sutras of Panini. The genitive case or shashţhi denotes many sorts of relations in Sanskrit, such as causation, possession, relation in place, comparison, nearness, proximity, change, collection, component member, &c. So that when a word is in the genitive case in a sutra generally, the doubt may arise in what sense that genitive is to be used. This aphorism lays down the restrictive rule for the interpretation of such words. It says that the force of such genitive is to convey the meaning of 'in the place of.' Thus in the sutra 34, the word इकः is in the genitive case; the literal translation being "of ik there is guņa and vṛiddhi." But "of" here means by virtue of the present rule of interpretation "in the place of." So that the sutra means 'in the place of ik'. The word स्थानम् here is synonymous with प्रसङ्ग or 'occasion.' Thus in the sentence दर्भाणां स्थाने शरैः प्रस्तरितव्यम् the word sthane, means 'prasange' i. e. wherever there is occasion to spread darbha grass, spread there the śara instead. Similarly in sūtras अस्तेर्भूः (II. 4. 52 S. 2470), or ब्रुवो वचिः (II. 4. 53 S. 2453), the words 'asti,' and 'bru' are in the genitive case, and mean, 'wherever there arises occasion to use the verbs अस् or ब्रू use there the verbs भू or वच् instead respectively.' Thus भविता, भवितुम्, भवितव्यम् are the future, gerund and passive participle respectively of अस् ; so also, वक्ता, वक्तुम् and वक्तव्यम् are the same forms of ब्रू. The word स्थानेयोगा is a bahuvrihi compound of two words, not in apposition, (vyadhikaraṇa bahuvrîhi, see II. 2. 24 and 35), and it qualifies the word shashṭhî. The compound means ‹?›, 'that which assumes the peculiar relation denoted by the word sthâna.' Consequently the seventh case-affix is not elided in this compound; on the analogy of compounds like ‹?› &c. Or ‹?›, the ए in sthâne is anomalous.

pk: 39. When a conon tern is obtained as a substitute, the likest or its signiricates to that in the place or which it cones, is the actual substitute. There are rour sorts or prolinity or nearnes :-(1) nearnes in place or ‹?› ( i. e. palate, throat &c. ); (2) nearnes in neaning or ‹?› (such as, singular terninations to be used arter words used in the sense or singular); (3) nearnes in quantity or ‹?› (such as a short vowel to replace a short vowel, a long vowel, a long one); (4) nearnes in quality or ‹?› (such as aspirates to replace aspirates, and sonants to replace sonants). Or al these aprolinates the rirst vis., the nearnes in the organ or uterance has prererence, in the selection or proper substitute. Thus in aplying rule Vi. 1. 101, s. 85 " when a honogeneous vowel rolows ak, the coresponding long vowel is the substitute ror both,” we nust have recourse to the present sûtra ror rinding the proper vowel. Thus in rinding the guna substitutes or ‹?› and ‹?› out or the thre guņa leters ‹?›, and ‹?›, we rind that ‹?› is a prolinate substitute having regard to prosodial neasure, i, e. ‹?› and ‹?› and ‹?› have al one nâtrâ ; while having regard to the prolinity or the organ or uterance, we get ‹?› and ‹?› ; the later however prevails to the elclusion or the rirst; as, ‹?›.
ck: 39. then a conon tern is optainet as a supstitute, the likest or its sikniricates to that in the place or thich it cones, is the actual supstitute. there are rour sorts or prolinity or nearnes :-(1) nearnes in place or ‹?› ( i. e. palate, throat &c. ); (2) nearnes in neanink or ‹?› (such as, sinkular terninations to pe uset arter torts uset in the sense or sinkular); (3) nearnes in tuantity or ‹?› (such as a short votel to replace a short votel, a lonk votel, a lonk one); (4) nearnes in tuality or ‹?› (such as aspirates to replace aspirates, ant sonants to replace sonants). s: 39. When a common term is obtained as a substitute, the likest of its significates to that in the place of which it comes, is the actual substitute. There are four sorts of proximity or nearness :-(1) nearness in place or ‹?› ( i. e. palate, throat &c. ); (2) nearness in meaning or ‹?› (such as, singular terminations to be used after words used in the sense of singular); (3) nearness in quantity or ‹?› (such as a short vowel to replace a short vowel, a long vowel, a long one); (4) nearness in quality or ‹?› (such as aspirates to replace aspirates, and sonants to replace sonants). Of all these approximates the first viz., the nearness in the organ of utterance has preference, in the selection of proper substitute. Thus in applying rule VI. 1. 101, S. 85 " when a homogeneous vowel follows ak, the corresponding long vowel is the substitute for both,” we must have recourse to the present sûtra for finding the proper vowel. Thus- दण्ड + ‹?› ; here the substitution of the long ‹?›, for the two short ‹?›'s, is an example of substitution by nearness of place, for both ‹?› and ‹?› are gutturals. Wherever there exist several kinds of proximity between that for which something else shall be substituted, and its possible substitutes, there the proximity as to the organ of speech is weightier than the rest, i. e., there that only is substituted which is nearest as regards the organs of speech with which both are uttered. Thus in finding the guna substitutes of ‹?› and ‹?› out of the three guņa letters ‹?›, and ‹?›, we find that ‹?› is a proximate substitute having regard to prosodial measure, i, e. ‹?› and ‹?› and ‹?› have all one mâtrâ ; while having regard to the proximity of the organ of utterance, we get ‹?› and ‹?› ; the latter however prevails to the exclusion of the first; as, ‹?›.

pk: 40. When a tern is elhibited in the seventh case in these sutras, the operation directed, is to be understod as arecting the state or what inediately precedes that which the tern denotes. This is a declaratory or interpreting sûtra. When in a sûtra, a word is used in the locative case, the operation ordained by that sûtra is to be perorned on the word preceding it. ck: 40. then a tern is elhipitet in the seventh case in these sutras, the operation tirectet, is to pe unterstot as arectink the state or that inetiately precetes that thich the tern tenotes. this is a teclaratory or interpretink sûtra. then in a sûtra, a tort is uset in the locative case, the operation ortainet py that sûtra is to pe perornet on the tort precetink it. thus in the sutra ‹?› (Vi. 1. 7. s. 47) the tort is in the locative case, thich sutra, thererore, neans that ‹?› rolotet py a votel (‹?›) are chanket into (‹?›). the literal translation or the sûtra peink : Or ‹?› there is ‹?›. the rorce or in or the locative case peink to intuce chankes in the leter precetink the votel. thus tati + utakan = tatyutakan so ‹?› pacatyotanan

This is a declaratory or interpreting sûtra. When in a sûtra, a word is used in the locative case, the operation ordained by that sûtra is to be performed on the word preceding it. Thus in the sutra ‹?› (VI. 1. 77. S. 47) the word is in the locative case, which sutra, therefore, means that ‹?› followed by a vowel (‹?›) are changed into (‹?›). The literal translation of the sûtra being : Of ‹?› there is ‹?›. The force of 'in' or the locative case being to induce changes in the letter preceding the vowel. Thus दधि + उदकम् = दध्युदकम् so ‹?› पचत्योदनम्

pk: 41. an operation caused by the elhibition or a tern in the ablative or rirth case, is to be understod to enjoin the substitution or sonething in the ron or that which inediately rolows the word denoted by the tern. This sutra elplains the rorce or words in the ablative case when enployed in these aphorisns. as the locative case rerers to a preceding word, so the ablative rerers to a suceding word. s: 41. An operation caused by the exhibition of a term in the ablative or fifth case, is to be understood to enjoin the substitution of something in the room of that which immediately follows the word denoted by the term. This sutra explains the force of words in the ablative case when employed in these aphorisms. As the locative case refers to a preceding word, so the ablative refers to a succeeding word. Thus sutra VIII. 4. 61, S. 118 declares that 'after ‹?›, of stha and stambha, the substitute is a letter belonging to the class of the prior.' Thus ‹?›. Here the word ‹?› is exhibited in the original sutra in the ablative case, and by the present sutra it means that a dental letter must be substituted in the place of stha, and by I. 1. 54, S. 44 this dental takes the place of ‹?› we have उद् + थ्थानम् = उत्थानम्.

pk: 43. and the substitute which has an indicatory na (even though it consists or nore than one leter) takes the place or the rinal leter only or the original elpresion. This sutra is an elception by anticipation to sutra i. 1. 5, s. 45. By that al substitutes, consisting or nore than one leter, replace the whole word. Thus in rorning the dvandva conpound or natr and pitr there is a rule (Vi. 3. 25, s. 921) by which it is declared:—in the place or words ending in r there is the substitution or anan in rorning dvandvas. now the substitute anan is a nit substitute, and thererore it aplies to the last leter or the word natr and not to the whole word, vis., the r or natr is only changed into an and not the whole word; and we have the conpound natapitarO, so also hotapotarO.
ck: 43. ant the supstitute thich has an inticatory na (even thoukh it consists or nore than one leter) takes the place or the rinal leter only or the orikinal elpresion. this sutra is an elception py anticipation to sutra i. 1. 5, s. 45. py that al supstitutes, consistink or nore than one leter, replace the thole tort. thus in rornink the tvantva conpount or natr ant pitr there is a rule (Vi. 3. 25, s. 921) py thich it is teclaret:—in the place or torts entink in r there is the supstitution or anan in rornink tvantvas. not the supstitute anan is a nit supstitute, ant thererore it aplies to the last leter or the tort natr ant not to the thole tort, vis., the r or natr is only chanket into an ant not the thole tort; ant te have the conpount natapitarO, so also hotapotarO.
s: 43. And the substitute which has an indicatory ङ (even though it consists of more than one letter) takes the place of the final letter only of the original expression. This sutra is an exception by anticipation to sutra I. 1. 55, S. 45. By that all substitutes, consisting of more than one letter, replace the whole word. Thus in forming the dvandva compound of मातृ and पितृ there is a rule (VI. 3. 25, S. 921) by which it is declared:—'In the place of words ending in ऋ there is the substitution of आनङ् in forming dvandvas.' Now the substitute आनङ् is a ङित् substitute, and therefore it applies to the last letter of the word मातृ and not to the whole word, viz., the ऋ of मातृ is only changed into आन् and not the whole word; and we have the compound मातापितरौ, so also होतापोतारौ.

pk: 4. That which is enjoined to cone in the ron or what rolows is to be understod as coning in the ron only or the rirst leter thereor. When any operation is to be nade in a word rolowing another, such operation is to be nade in the initial leter or such subsequent word. This is an elception to sûtra i. 1. 52, s. 42 (alontyasya). To give an ilustration:—there is a rule (Vi. 3. 97, s. 941) by which it is declared: in the place or ap used arter the words dvi and antara and the particles caled upasarga there is it. This rule nay be stated in other words as:—in the place or ap there is it when ap rolows dvi or antara. now it is clear that it is not to replace al the leters or ap but only one. By sûtra 42 that leter would have ben the last leter or ap, but this sûtra nakes an elception, nanely, where an operation is directed to be nade in a word, sinply by reason or its being placed arter another word; such change is to be nade in the begining or such second word. Thererore, the i replaces the a or ap and we have dvi + ip = dvipa (the rinal a is aded by V. 4. 74, s. 940) an island, pronontory.
ck: 4. that thich is encoinet to cone in the ron or that rolots is to pe unterstot as conink in the ron only or the rirst leter thereor. then any operation is to pe nate in a tort rolotink another, such operation is to pe nate in the initial leter or such supsetuent tort. this is an elception to sûtra i. 1. 52, s. 42 (alontyasya). to kive an ilustration:—there is a rule (Vi. 3. 97, s. 941) py thich it is teclaret: in the place or ap uset arter the torts tvi ant antara ant the particles calet upasarka there is it. this rule nay pe statet in other torts as:—in the place or ap there is it then ap rolots tvi or antara. not it is clear that it is not to replace al the leters or ap put only one. py sûtra 42 that leter toult have pen the last leter or ap, put this sûtra nakes an elception, nanely, there an operation is tirectet to pe nate in a tort, sinply py reason or its peink placet arter another tort; such chanke is to pe nate in the pekinink or such secont tort. thererore, the i replaces the a or ap ant te have tvi + ip = tvipa (the rinal a is atet py V. 4. 74, s. 940) an islant, pronontory.
s: 44. That which is enjoined to come in the room of what follows is to be understood as coming in the room only of the first letter thereof. When any operation is to be made in a word following another, such operation is to be made in the initial letter of such subsequent word. This is an exception to sûtra I. 1. 52, S. 42 (अलोऽन्त्यस्य). To give an illustration:—there is a rule (VI. 3. 97, S. 941) by which it is declared: 'In the place of अप् used after the words द्वि and अन्तर and the particles called उपसर्ग there is ईत्.' This rule may be stated in other words as:—'In the place of अप् there is ईत् when अप् follows द्वि or अन्तर.' Now it is clear that ईत् is not to replace all the letters of अप् but only one. By sûtra 42 that letter would have been the last letter of अप्, but this sûtra makes an exception, namely, where an operation is directed to be made in a word, simply by reason of its being placed after another word; such change is to be made in the beginning of such second word. Therefore, the ई replaces the अ of अप् and we have द्वि + ईप् = द्वीप (the final अ is added by V. 4. 74, S. 940) 'an island,' 'promontory.'

pk: 45. a substitute consisting or nore than one leter, and a substitute having an indicatory s take the place or the whole or the original elpresion elhibited in the silth case. This sutra is an elception to sûtra i. 1. 52, s. 42 by which it was declared that an âdeśa or substitute replaces only the last leter. This sûtra on the contrary enjoins that an âdeśa consisting or nore than one leter replaces the whole elpresion in the genitive case, and not only its last leter. Even where an âdeśa consists or a single leter, but ir it has a s as its indicatory leter, it replaces the whole word. Thus, there is a sûtra bruvo vaci (i. 4. 53, s. 2453) which neans in the place or bru let there be vac. ere the âdeśa consists or thre leters (nore than one), and thererore, it replaces the whole word and not only the last leter. That is to say in rorning certain tenses the verb bru is replaced by vac. Thus the ruture tense or bru is vaksyati he wil speak. Thus in the sutra aswaBya Os (Vi. 1. 21, s. 372) arter the sten aswan, Os is substituted ror the ending or the noninative and acusative plural. The substitute Os is a sit substitute and thererore it replaces the whole or the ariles jas and sas and not only their initials as would have ben otherwise required by the preceding rule ade parasya. ror by that rule the initials only or the ariles jas and sas would have ben replaced by O. This sûtra is in ract an elception to the last sutra.
ck: 45. a supstitute consistink or nore than one leter, ant a supstitute havink an inticatory s take the place or the thole or the orikinal elpresion elhipitet in the silth case. this sutra is an elception to sûtra i. 1. 52, s. 42 py thich it tas teclaret that an âteśa or supstitute replaces only the last leter. this sûtra on the contrary encoins that an âteśa consistink or nore than one leter replaces the thole elpresion in the kenitive case, ant not only its last leter. Even there an âteśa consists or a sinkle leter, put ir it has a s as its inticatory leter, it replaces the thole tort. thus, there is a sûtra pruvo vaci (i. 4. 53, s. 2453) thich neans in the place or pru let there pe vac. ere the âteśa consists or thre leters (nore than one), ant thererore, it replaces the thole tort ant not only the last leter. that is to say in rornink certain tenses the verp pru is replacet py vac. thus the ruture tense or pru is vaksyati he til speak. thus in the sutra astapya Os (Vi. 1. 21, s. 372) arter the sten astan, Os is supstitutet ror the entink or the noninative ant acusative plural. the supstitute Os is a sit supstitute ant thererore it replaces the thole or the ariles cas ant sas ant not only their initials as toult have pen othertise retuiret py the precetink rule ate parasya. ror py that rule the initials only or the ariles cas ant sas toult have pen replacet py O. this sûtra is in ract an elception to the last sutra.
s: 45. A substitute consisting of more than one letter, and a substitute having an indicatory श् take the place of the whole of the original expression exhibited in the sixth case. This sutra is an exception to sûtra I. 1. 52, S. 42 by which it was declared that an âdeśa or substitute replaces only the last letter. This sûtra on the contrary enjoins that an âdeśa consisting of more than one letter replaces the whole expression in the genitive case, and not only its last letter. Even where an âdeśa consists of a single letter, but if it has a श् as its indicatory letter, it replaces the whole word. Thus, there is a sûtra ब्रुवो वचिः (II. 4. 53, S. 2453) which means 'in the place of ब्रू let there be वच्.' Here the âdeśa consists of three letters (more than one), and therefore, it replaces the whole word and not only the last letter. That is to say in forming certain tenses the verb ब्रू is replaced by वच्. Thus the future tense of ब्रू is वक्ष्यति 'he will speak.' Thus in the sutra अष्टाभ्य औश् (VII. 1. 21, S. 372) 'after the stem अष्टन्, औश् is substituted for the ending of the Nominative and Accusative plural.' The substitute औश् is a शित् substitute and therefore it replaces the whole of the affixes जस् and शस् and not only their initials as would have been otherwise required by the preceding rule आदेः परस्य. For by that rule the initials only of the affixes जस् and शस् would have been replaced by औ. This sûtra is in fact an exception to the last sutra.

pk: 46. in these aphorisns, when a word is narked with a svarita acent, by that an adhikāra or a governing rule is to be understod. When in this colection or granatical sutras, there is any sûtra that has a circunrlel acent, it denotes that it is either the begining or a subject and the subsequent sûtras are governed by it, or that it ends a subject and separates the previous sutras ron the rolowing. as a rule, the sûtras are not narked with acents; it is thererore ron conentaries that one has to learn whether a sutra has a svarita or not. Thus the rolowing sutras, nust evidently have svarita as they are governing sûtras; pratyaya (i. 1. 1, s. 180), Dato (i. 1. 91, s. 2829), angasya (Vi. 4. 1, s. 20), Basya (Vi. 4. 129, s. 23). Paribhāshā.—Or (these rour kinds or rules,—vis.) a subsequent (rule,) a nitya (rule), an antaraṅga (rule), and an apavāda (rule), each rolowing rule poseses greater rorce than any one or, or al, the rules nentioned berore it. note:—By i. 4. 2, s. 175, we are taught that a subsequent (para) rule supersedes a rule which precedes (purva). Thus i. 1. 7, s. 2534, Vikaraṇa berore sārvadhātuka; (nitya) Vi. 3. 86, s. 2189, Guṇa ror u (para but anitya). i. 1. 7, s. 2534, aplies berore the substitution or guṇa ror u, and it would aply also ir guṇa were substituted ror u, and ir tud were changed to tod. On the other hand Vi. 3. 86 aplies berore sa is aded to tud, but arter the adition or sa to tud guṇa could not by Vi. 3. 86 be substituted ror u, because the later would have ceased to be penultinate. acordingly i. 1. 7 is nitya and Vi. 3. 86 is anitya; i. 1. 7 takes, thererore, erect rirst and we have tud + sa + ti, and subsequently Vi. 3. 86 is no longer aplicable. a nitya is thus derined:—a rule which would aply ir another rule that aplies sinultaneously were to have taken erect, and which aplies when that other rule does not take erect, is nitya; a rule with which such is not the case, is not nitya. an antaraṅga rule poseses

On the other hant Vi. 3. 86 aplies perore sa is atet to tut, put arter the atition or sa to tut kuṇa coult not py Vi. 3. 86 pe supstitutet ror u, pecause the later toult have ceaset to pe penultinate. acortinkly i. 1. 7 is nitya ant Vi. 3. 86 is anitya; i. 1. 7 takes, thererore, erect rirst ant te have tut + sa + ti, ant supsetuently Vi. 3. 86 is no lonker aplicaple. a nitya is thus terinet:—a rule thich toult aply ir another rule that aplies sinultaneously tere to have taken erect, ant thich aplies then that other rule toes not take erect, is nitya; a rule tith thich such is not the case, is not nitya. an antaraṅka rule poseses kreate
s: 46. In these aphorisms, when a word is marked with a svarita accent, by that an adhikāra or a governing rule is to be understood. When in this collection of grammatical sutras, there is any sûtra that has a circumflex accent, it denotes that it is either the beginning of a subject and the subsequent sûtras are governed by it, or that it ends a subject and separates the previous sutras from the following. As a rule, the sûtras are not marked with accents; it is therefore from commentaries that one has to learn whether a sutra has a svarita or not. Thus the following sutras, must evidently have svarita as they are governing sûtras; प्रत्ययः (III. 1. 1, S. 180), धातोः (III. 1. 91, S. 2829), अङ्गस्य (VI. 4. 1, S. 200), भस्य (VI. 4. 129, S. 233). Paribhāshā.—Of (these four kinds of rules,—viz.) a subsequent (rule,) a nitya (rule), an antaraṅga (rule), and an apavāda (rule), each following rule possesses greater force than any one of, or all, the rules mentioned before it. Note:—By I. 4. 2, S. 175, we are taught that a subsequent (पर) rule supersedes a rule which precedes (पूर्व). This Paribhāshā further expands the same. A nitya rule is stronger than a Para (पर) rule. As तुदादिभ्यः शः (III. 1. 77, S. 2534) तुदति; रुधादिभ्यः श्नम् (III. 1. 78, S. 2543) as रुणद्धि. Here the nitya affixes श and श्नम् debar even the पर rule of Guṇa of the light penultimate vowel of VII. 3. 86, S. 2189. Similarly ‹?› and ‹?›. Here the augment ‹?› by III. 4. 92, S. 2204 being a nitya rule supersedes even the subsequent (पर) rule VI. 4. 107, S. 2333 which required the elision of the ‹हि› of ‹सिप्› before the affixes ‹?› and ‹?›. Thus III. 1. 77, S. 2534, Vikaraṇa before Sārvadhātuka; (nitya) VII. 3. 86, S. 2189, Guṇa for उ (para but anitya). III. 1. 77, S. 2534, applies before the substitution of guṇa for उ, and it would apply also if guṇa were substituted for उ, and if तुद् were changed to तोद्. On the other hand VII. 3. 86 applies before श is added to तुद्, but after the addition of श to तुद् guṇa could not by VII. 3. 86 be substituted for उ, because the latter would have ceased to be penultimate. Accordingly III. 1. 77 is nitya and VII. 3. 86 is anitya; III. 1. 77 takes, therefore, effect first and we have तुद् + श + ति, and subsequently VII. 3. 86 is no longer applicable. A nitya is thus defined:—A rule which would apply if another rule that applies simultaneously were to have taken effect, and which applies when that other rule does not take effect, is nitya; a rule with which such is not the case, is not nitya. An antaraṅga rule possesses greater force than even a nitya rule. Antaraṅga is a rule the causes of the application of which lie within (or before) the sum of the causes of a bahiraṅga rule; in like manner that rule the causes of the application of which lie without or beyond the sum of the causes of that antaraṅga rule is bahiraṅga. In the formation of a nom. dual of the neuter noun ‹वारी›, we have two rules, first VII. 1. 73, S. 320, by which ‹नुँम्› is added before the dual case affix शी; and I. 2. 47, S. 318, which requires the shortening of the stem ‹वारी› to वारि. Though the augment ‹नुँम्› is nitya, it is for the time being suspended in favour of the antaraṅga rule causing shortening and when the stem is shortened then the ‹नुँम्› is added. For had ‹नुँम्› been added first, then ‹वारिन्› would end in a consonant and the rule of shortening I. 2. 47, S. 318 would not have applied, as the stem was not vowel-ending. An apavāda possesses greater force even than an antaraṅga rule. A rule which is given in reference to a particular case or particular cases, to which or to all of which another rule can not but apply, or in other words which all fall already under some other rule, supersedes the latter. Thus ‹?›, here the antaranga rules ‹?› and ‹?› would supersede even the rule of savarna-dirgha, and ‹?› + ‹?› would be ‹?› But savarṇa-dirgha rule being an apavâda rule supersedes the antaranga guna and yan-âdesa. Paribhasha.—That which is bahir

pk: 47. The senivowels y, v, r, l, are the substitutes or the coresponding vowels i, u, r and l (long and short), when rolowed by a vowel. This sûtra is rather to wide. it nust be restricted by Vi. 1. 101, s. 85 nanely, the rolowing vowel nust not be or the sane clas as the preceding, ror the aplication or this rule. Thus suDi + upasya ere the long i or suDi is replaced by y which is the nearest substitute, having regard to sthana or organ or uterance. Thus we get suDy + upasya This gives ocasion to the aplication or the rolowing rule requiring reduplication :-
ck: 47. the senivotels y, v, r, l, are the supstitutes or the corespontink votels i, u, r ant l (lonk ant short), then rolotet py a votel. this sûtra is rather to tite. it nust pe restrictet py Vi. 1. 101, s. 85 nanely, the rolotink votel nust not pe or the sane clas as the precetink, ror the aplication or this rule. thus suti + upasya ere the lonk i or suti is replacet py y thich is the nearest supstitute, havink rekart to sthana or orkan or uterance. thus te ket suty + upasya this kives ocasion to the aplication or the rolotink rule retuirink retuplication :-
s: 47. The semivowels य्, व्, र्, ल्, are the substitutes of the corresponding vowels इ, उ, ऋ and ऌ (long and short), when followed by a vowel. This sûtra is rather too wide. It must be restricted by VI. 1. 101, S. 85 namely, the following vowel must not be of the same class as the preceding, for the application of this rule. Thus सुधी + उपास्यः Here the long ई of सुधी is replaced by य् which is the nearest substitute, having regard to sthana or organ of utterance. Thus we get सुध्य् + उपास्य This gives occasion to the application of the following rule requiring reduplication :--

pk: 48. When a vowel does not rolow, there is optionaly reduplication or yara (al the consonants elcept ha), arter a vowel. Thererore, the leter D is doubled, and we have :- su D D y + upasya now, a doubt arises as to the aplicability or this rule or doubling by the rolowing consideration :-
